Dear authors,

Thank you for responding to my questions.
>Meanwhile, we think another compelling avenue for future research is zero-shot generalization with LLMs, which could potentially eliminate the need for a large dedicated training set

Even without the need for a large training dataset, we would still require access to a dataset with many tasks on a large number of websites to evaluate and assess the model's generalization capabilities. I therefore appreciate that the authors are planning to expand the dataset, since there is a need for large and varied datasets if the goal is a generalist agent.

That being said, this dataset is a significant improvement compared to existing datasets in this domain and I am confident that it will be an invaluable resource for the community.

Thank you for taking the time to review our work and for providing valuable feedback for improvement! Here are some additional details which we hope could address your concerns:

- *Compare against existing models*

We greatly appreciate your valuable feedback, and we agree that a comparison with existing methods would certainly enhance the work. However, due to the complex nature of Mind2Web, particularly its long and noisy web pages, most existing methods aren't directly applicable. With this in mind, we are reaching out to other researchers to see if we can acquire relevant code/models such as WebN-T5 [1] (Understanding HTML with Large Language Models) and their help with evaluation on Mind2Web. We hope that Mind2Web will become a standard benchmark for assessing the performance of web agents, and we welcome more people to test their methods against it.

- *Low performance on held-out websites*

Yes, we agree that the performance of existing models on held-out websites and domains are definitely still far from satisfactory, even for LLMs. One thing to note though is that all the models that we have tested have not been specifically pre-trained for HTML documents or taking actions on web pages (at least based on public information that we know). Mind2Web is primarily designed as a testing dataset to assess the performance of web agents, especially their ability to generalize across environments. We think the low performance actually reflects the diversity and challenging nature of Mind2Web as an evaluation dataset. 

Due to budget constraints, we acknowledge that the training set of Mind2Web is still limited at the moment. We do have all the tools ready to expand the dataset and intend to do so as resources permit. Meanwhile, we think another compelling avenue for future research is zero-shot generalization with LLMs, which could potentially eliminate the need for a large dedicated training set. We have already seen promising results with GPT-4, and how to further improve these LLMs, and build more powerful web agents in self-supervised fashion is something that we think definitely worth more exploration.

- Thanks for bringing to our attention the missing mentioning of a detailed maintenance plan in the paper.  The authors and the OSU NLP group are committed to ensuring its regular upkeep and updates.

[1] Gur, Izzeddin, Ofir Nachum, Yingjie Miao, Mustafa Safdari, Austin Huang, Aakanksha Chowdhery, Sharan Narang, Noah Fiedel and Aleksandra Faust. “Understanding HTML with Large Language Models.” ArXiv abs/2210.03945 (2022).

Thank you for taking the time to thoroughly review our work and for your praise! Your suggestions for potential improvements are highly valued, and we'd like to offer some additional details on how we plan to incorporate each of them in the revised version.

- *Additional results showcasing performance comparison of various methods on the subset that GPT-4 is tested on*.

Here is the step success rate results for other methods on the 50 test examples that GPT-4 is tested on, numbers in parentheses are the results on the full test set (same as table 2 in the paper) :

|model|Cross-Task|Cross-Website|Cross-Domain|
|--|--|--|--|
|flan-t5-base |43.3 (41.0)|25.3 (29.5)|28.1 (31.6)|
|flan-t5-large |48.1 (50.3)|30.8 (35.3)|27.6 (37.3)|
|flan-t5-xl |47.9 (52.0)|33.3 (38.9)|34.6 (39.6)|
|gpt-3.5 	|15.2 (17.4)|15.1 (16.2)|16.7 (18.6)|
|gpt-4 	|36.2       |30.1       |26.4|

As we can see, the results on the 50 test samples are consistent with the results on the respective full test set, and the relative performance across methods and splits remains the same.

- *Flan-T5-xl in zero-shot setting*.

Since flan-t5 is tuned with multi-choice format, it can only do element selection in zero-shot. Here we report element accuracy. As reference, results for the tuned model are shown in parentheses.

|model|Cross-Task|Cross-Website|Cross-Domain|
|--|--|--|--|
flan-t5-xl|10.8 (52.0)		|7.8 (38.9)		|11.7 (39.6)

As we can see, while the model still gets some elements correct, it is much lower compared to the fine-tuned model, and 3-shot GPT 3.5/4. This is expected, since Flan-T5 is not tuned for HTML and coding related tasks.

- *Code and model*

Our code and models are available now in our github repo: https://github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/Mind2Web

- *Results on existing datasets*

Thanks for the suggestion! This is a very interesting idea! Given the differences in experimental setup and applicability of some baseline methods, we did not directly compare results on Mind2Web with other existing datasets in the paper. However, in the recent AgentBench paper [1], the authors compare results of existing LLMs on Mind2Web, Webshop and some other agent-centric datasets. From their results, we can see that Mind2Web is indeed more challenging even for most state-of-art methods. Benchmarking performance of different models across datasets is definitely something worth further exploring.

- *General backgrounds of LLM*

Thank you for pointing out the missing discussion on large language models in the related work section. We concur that given NeurIPS' wide-reaching audience, a general introduction to LLMs is definitely beneficial. We will make sure to add this in the revised version.

[1] Liu, Xiao, Hao Yu, Hanchen Zhang, Yifan Xu, Xuanyu Lei, Hanyu Lai, Yu Gu et al. "AgentBench: Evaluating LLMs as Agents." arXiv preprint arXiv:2308.03688 (2023).

Thank you for acknowledging our efforts and for your thoughtful feedback! We are in complete agreement about the importance of ethical and responsible use for developing web agents, which led to our discussion on this matter at the end of the supplementary material. The evolution and capabilities of large language models nowadays,  as evident from zero-shot experiments with GPT-4, make it even more pertinent for the community to address the responsible usage of these techniques. Perhaps, a dedicated paper on this topic is in order. With Mind2Web, we hope it to not only facilitate the community in building more powerful web agents but also inspire deeper reflections on potential societal impacts.

- Regarding  *“ensure the data quality and diversity”*, the tasks in the dataset are carefully reviewed by the authors after being proposed by the annotators. We rejected queries that lack diversity and imposed limitations on the number of tasks from each annotator and for each website. A post-annotation verification round is also conducted to remove unsatisfactory samples and standardize the annotated traces. However, as stated in the appendix under limitations, the dataset is primarily gathered via MTurk and centers on U.S. websites. We are already equipped with an annotation tool, and expanding both website and annotator diversity is an avenue we intend to explore next as resources allow.

- Regarding *“dynamic or personalized web content”*, our dataset comprises live websites and tasks/traces from multiple users. This design enables us to train and evaluate agents that perform well in dynamic real-world environments.  We agree that advancements can be made in modeling to better manage dynamic web interactions. Incorporating models with better long-context handling or equipped with memory are promising directions for future work.

- Regarding *“existing guidelines or best practices for web automation or web data collection”*, thank you for the valuable suggestion! We are actually inspired by and have closely followed established methodologies from existing works such as MiniWoB[1], CommonCrawl[2], WebShop[3], Rico[4] and MoTIF[5]. If you have any other resources to recommend, we would be most appreciative. We would also like to note that since existing guidelines are mostly geared towards traditional web crawling methods, the question of how to regulate more sophisticated web agents powered by machine learning is an area that surely warrants further investigation.

- Regarding Item 3 in *“Opportunities For Improvement”*, we would be truly grateful if you could be more specific and provide further suggestions on what additional analyses and experiments related to data/model we could include to enhance our work.

[1] Shi, Tianlin, Andrej Karpathy, Linxi Fan, Jonathan Hernandez, and Percy Liang. "World of bits: An open-domain platform for web-based agents." In International Conference on Machine Learning, pp. 3135-3144. PMLR, 2017.

[2] CommonCrawl https://commoncrawl.org

[3] Yao, Shunyu, Howard Chen, John Yang, and Karthik Narasimhan. "Webshop: Towards scalable real-world web interaction with grounded language agents." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 35 (2022): 20744-20757.

[4] Deka, Biplab, Zifeng Huang, Chad Franzen, Joshua Hibschman, Daniel Afergan, Yang Li, Jeffrey Nichols, and Ranjitha Kumar. "Rico: A mobile app dataset for building data-driven design applications." In Proceedings of the 30th annual ACM symposium on user interface software and technology, pp. 845-854. 2017.

[5] Burns, Andrea, Deniz Arsan, Sanjna Agrawal, Ranjitha Kumar, Kate Saenko, and Bryan A. Plummer. "A dataset for interactive vision-language navigation with unknown command feasibility." In European Conference on Computer Vision, pp. 312-328. Cham: Springer Nature Switzerland, 2022.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces MIND2WEB, a novel dataset for creating and assessing versatile web agents capable of executing complex tasks on any website using language instructions. Overcoming limitations of existing datasets, MIND2WEB offers over 2,000 tasks from 137 real-world websites across 31 domains, and allows for a wide spectrum of user interaction patterns. The authors also propose a two-stage model, MINDACT, which filters web elements using a smaller language model and then uses a large language model to select from the filtered elements. While promising results are achieved, the authors recognize the need for further improvements towards creating truly generalist web agents. The datasets, code, and models are released as well.

strengths.value:
1. The idea to construct this benchmark is very interesting, i.e., evaluating the ability of LLM-based agent to follow complex instructions in the web.

2. The dataset and tasks are impressively diverse and comprehensive, which can provide challenges for LLM.

3. The authors have made corresponding materials, including datasets, models, and codes, publically, which can help followers to continue this research.

opportunities_for_improvement.value: Generally speaking, I do not find any evident limitations of this work.

title.value: This paper presents a new dataset, MIND2WEB, for developing and evaluating general-purpose web agents capable of performing complex tasks on any website based on linguistic instructions.

confidence.value: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper presents an interesting dataset with a challenging research problem. The dataset proposed in this paper is for developing and evaluating generalist agents for the web that can follow language instructions to complete complex tasks on any website, which is an useful and timely research topic for LLM Agents. This paper also proposes a generic web agent model MINDACT based on a Large Language Model (LLM), which uses a Small Language Model (LM) to filter web page elements and then a LLM to predict the operations of the filtered elements.  The paper evaluates MINDACT and several baselines on MIND2WEB under different generalization settings and analyzes the results. This model shows some effectiveness on the dataset, especially in terms of its ability to generalize across websites and domains.

strengths.value:
1. It presents a novel and challenging task of building generalist agents for the web, which has many potential applications and benefits for web users and language models.

2. It creates a large-scale and diverse dataset that covers 137 websites from 31 domains, with over 2000 open-ended tasks and crowdsourced action sequences, as well as rich web snapshots and interaction traces.

3. It proposes an effective and efficient model that combines a small LM for candidate generation and an LLM for action prediction, and shows that it can achieve decent performance and generalization across domains, websites, and tasks.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. The evaluation metrics are based on the exact matching of elements and operations, which may not capture the partial correctness or semantic similarity of the predictions.

2. The ethical and social implications of the task and the dataset are not adequately discussed.

3. It does not adequately analyze and compare related work, does not provide adequate statistics and analysis of the dataset, and does not provide adequate experiments and analysis of the model.

limitations.value: The authors have briefly mentioned some limitations and potential negative societal impact of their work, but they have not provided sufficient details or suggestions on how to address them. For example, they could discuss how to ensure the data quality and diversity, how to handle dynamic or personalized web content, etc. They could also refer to existing guidelines or best practices for web automation or web data collection.

correctness.value: I have visited the website provided by the authors and checked the details of their dataset, code, and models. Based on that, I found that the claims made in the submission are correct. The dataset is constructed in a sound way, with a clear methodology, statistics, and quality control. The benchmark design is appropriate and performed correctly, with a comprehensive evaluation, analysis, and comparison. The authors also provide the full data, code, and models for reproducibility and accessibility. Therefore, I have no major concerns about the correctness or validity of their work.

clarity.value: The paper is well written overall, with clear structure, motivation, contribution, methodology, evaluation, analysis, and discussion. However, there are some typos, grammatical errors, or unclear expressions that need to be fixed.

relation_to_prior_work.value: The paper clearly discusses how this work differs from previous contributions by comparing with existing datasets and models for web agents or grounded language understanding. It also cites relevant literature throughout the paper to highlight the novelty and significance of this work.

documentation.value: For the dataset, the paper provides sufficient detail on data collection and organization in Section 2. In addition, the authors provide much detail on GitHub. However, it does not provide much detail on ethical and responsible use, such as how to prevent misuse or abuse of the data or the agents trained on it, etc. These aspects should be clarified in the paper or in a separate documentation file.

ethics.value: I do not suspect there is any ethical concerns with this submission.

summary_and_contributions.value: This paper introduces the Mind2Web dataset, which includes over 2000 complex tasks across multiple domains, designed to evaluate the capability of general agents in performing complex tasks. The authors also provide a baseline method and corresponding results. The website associated with this dataset is well-crafted.

strengths.value:
1. The proposed dataset Mind2Web is novel and challenging, focusing on an important research direction. The capability of general agents to solve complex tasks is getting more and more attention, especially in the LLMs era. The proposed dataset is a great resource to the community.
2. The paper presents necessary details about the dataset construction.
3. The associated project website and GitHub repository are well-crafted.
4. The paper is well-written and easy-to-follow.
5. A simple baseline method is introduced. Corresponding results are provided.
6. Comparisons between prior efforts and the proposed datasets are clear and comprehensive.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
1. Since the test sets vary, the results in Table 2 comparing GPT-4 to other methods may not be meaningful and may mislead the audience. It is recommended to present an additional table showcasing a performance comparison of various methods on this specific subset.
2. Results of Flan-T5 in a zero-shot setting are recommended to present for the convenience of comparing Flan-T5 w/ ChatGPT in a similar setting.
3. The code and models are not yet available.
4. It could be interesting if the results on existing datasets are also provided. This can quantitatively demonstrate why the Mind2Web dataset is more challenging and closer to reality.
5. It could be better to provide more general backgrounds of LLMs for audience with various backgrounds. For instance, consider referencing some survey papers [1].

[1] Zhao et al. A Survey of Large Language Models. https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.18223

title.value: Mind2Web is a large-scale dataset that represents a significant improvement compared to other related datasets in the field

confidence.value: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

summary_and_contributions.value:
The paper introduces the Mind2Web dataset, which is useful for training agents to complete tasks based on instructions on any website. The dataset consists of $137$ real websites from $31$ domains along with natural language task instructions that can be completed on these websites and that are formulated as high-level goals.

The authors also introduce MindAct, a two-stage training process for learning to complete tasks using both small and large language models (LM) over the web. The small LM is used in the first stage to identify a smaller set of candidate elements which are then processed by a large LM. MindAct is then evaluated on Mind2Web in three settings where the models are trained and then evaluated on either held-out domains, websites, or tasks.

strengths.value:
- The dataset is significantly larger and more suitable for generalization to new websites and domains compared to previous works that are geared towards learning to complete tasks over the web. Therefore, this dataset will be very valuable to the research community.
- The tasks are formulated as high-level goals instead of step-by-step instructions and are therefore more representative of what a user would task an agent with.
- They provide an interesting evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on this application.

opportunities_for_improvement.value:
- They do not compare MindAct against any previous models used for this task (for instance, [DOM-Q-Net](https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.07257)). It would have been interesting to see how the performance of the LLMs compared against previous works on the Mind2Web dataset.
- The dataset is supposed to be used for cross-domain and cross-website evaluation, however, the performance of MindAct is quite poor on held-out websites and domains. The step-success rate when evaluated on new websites and domains is rather low (38.9% and 39.6% success rate). This either suggests that the task is very challenging for LLMs or perhaps that the dataset is not large and varied enough for generalization to new websites and domains.

limitations.value: The authors have adequately addressed limitations and potential negative social impact in the Appendix.

correctness.value: All claims seem correct to me and the collection of the dataset seems sound.

relation_to_prior_work.value: They thoroughly review prior work and discuss how it relates to MIND2WEB. MIND2WEB represents a significant improvement compared to previous datasets for this application.

documentation.value: There are sufficient details in the main part of the submission, and additional information in the appendix about the dataset collection. The authors also provide a URL for accessing the dataset through huggingface.co. Here they provide information about the dataset structure and the dataset's train and test split. They also provide a license. I cannot find information about a maintenance plan.

ethics.value: I do not suspect that there are any ethical concerns with this submission.

flag_for_ethics_review.value: 2: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

title.value: Mind2Web: Towards a Generalist Agent for the Web

abstract.value: We introduce Mind2Web, the first dataset for developing and evaluating generalist agents for the web that can follow language instructions to complete complex tasks on any website. Existing datasets for web agents either use simulated websites or only cover a limited set of websites and tasks, thus not suitable for generalist web agents. With over 2,000 open-ended tasks collected from 137 websites spanning 31 domains and crowdsourced action sequences for the tasks, Mind2Web provides three necessary ingredients for building generalist web agents: 1) diverse domains, websites, and tasks, 2) use of real-world websites instead of simulated and simplified ones, and 3) a broad spectrum of user interaction patterns. Based on Mind2Web, we conduct an initial exploration of using large language models (LLMs) for building generalist web agents. While the raw HTML of real-world websites are often too large to be fed to LLMs, we show that first filtering it with a small LM significantly improves the effectiveness and efficiency of LLMs. Our solution demonstrates a decent level of performance, even on websites or entire domains the model has never seen before, but there is still a substantial room to improve towards truly generalizable agents. We open-source our dataset, model implementation, and trained models (https://osu-nlp-group.github.io/Mind2Web) to facilitate further research on building a generalist agent for the web.

TLDR.value: We introduce Mind2Web, the first dataset for developing and evaluating generalist agents for the web that can follow language instructions to complete complex tasks on any website.

dateprocesses.script:
def process(client, invitation):

    domain = client.get_group(invitation.domain)
    venue_id = domain.id
    submission_venue_id = domain.content['submission_venue_id']['value']
    venue_name = domain.content['title']['value']

    now = openreview.tools.datetime_millis(datetime.datetime.utcnow())
    cdate = invitation.cdate

    if cdate > now:
        ## invitation is in the future, do not process
        print('invitation is not yet active', cdate)
        return

    def post_submission_edit(submission):

        updated_note = openreview.api.Note(
            id=submission.id
        )

        if invitation.edit['note']['readers'] == ['everyone'] and submission.odate is None:
            updated_note.odate = now
            updated_note.content = {
                '_bibtex': {
                    'value': openreview.tools.generate_bibtex(
                        note=submission,
                        venue_fullname=venue_name,
                        year=str(datetime.datetime.utcnow().year),
                        url_forum=submission.forum,
                        paper_status='under review',
                        anonymous='readers' in submission.content['authors'] or 'readers' in invitation.edit.get('note', {}).get('content', {}).get('authors', {})
                    )
                }
            }

        client.post_note_edit(
            invitation=invitation.id,
            note=updated_note,
            signatures=[venue_id]
        )
    
    ## Release the submissions to specified readers if venueid is still submission
    submissions = client.get_all_notes(content= { 'venueid': submission_venue_id })
    print(f'update {len(submissions)} submissions')
    openreview.tools.concurrent_requests(post_submission_edit, submissions, desc='post_submission_edit')
